slides.headline: This desert lizard drinks through its skin.
slides.sub: Tiny grooves between its scales pipe water straight to its mouth

slides.headline: Plumbing built into its scales
slides.body: Grooves ring each spine and link up across its body. Capillary action draws water along them, even uphill, to the corners of its mouth.

slides.label: of its body weight in water, just to fill the channels
slides.body: Only once they are full can it drink. Standing in a puddle did it; damp sand alone filled them to about 59%.
slides.source: Comanns et al., J Exp Biol (2016)

slides.headline: So it shovels wet sand onto its back
slides.body: After rain, wild thorny devils have been seen heaping damp sand over themselves. Tests on skin replicas suggest sand on top can fill the channels.
slides.source: Comanns et al., J Exp Biol (2016)

slides.label: ants eaten a day, by one estimate
slides.body: It eats only ants, sitting beside their trails and picking them off one by one, at rates of up to one ant per second.

slides.headline: A decoy head for predators
slides.body: Threatened, it tucks its real head between its forelegs and presents a spiny knob on top: a 'false head' that makes it hard to swallow.

slides.headline: Send this to someone who forgets to drink water.
slides.body: One survival trick at a time, properly sourced. Follow @earthspirit_nature.
sources: Comanns, Withers, Esser & Baumgartner (2016) Cutaneous water collection by a moisture-harvesting lizard. J. Exp. Biol. 219:3473–3479
IUCN Red List: Moloch horridus, Least Concern (2017)

caption:
The thorny devil (Moloch horridus) drinks through its skin, wicking water along grooves between its scales to its mouth.

This small ant-eating lizard lives in the sandy deserts of inland Australia, where rain is rare. Once its skin channels are full, it drinks with small gulping jaw movements, taking in roughly 0.7 microlitres per gulp in lab tests. The same study found that dew and condensation alone probably cannot fill the channels, so rain and damp sand matter most. It is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (2017).

Swipe for how the plumbing works. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Comanns et al. (2016), Journal of Experimental Biology 219:3473–3479; Animal Diversity Web; IUCN Red List.

Keep this one for the next time someone says lizards are boring.
